title: Monitoring latency, tokens and cost
description: Track user-visible performance and resource usage with actionable alerts.
objectives: Choose useful latency and usage metrics
Connect alerts to an owner and an investigation path
explanation: Measure total request latency and component durations, including queueing, retrieval, generation, and tools. For streaming, track time to first output separately. Percentiles expose the slow tail that a mean can hide. Define whether failed and cancelled requests are included in each metric.

Record input and output usage from the provider where available, labeling estimates as estimates. Attach model and application versions without including sensitive prompts. Aggregate by a small set of meaningful dimensions; unbounded request IDs belong in traces, not metric label sets.

Define a service objective, then alert on sustained user impact rather than every isolated slow request. Combine latency, error rate, cost per accepted task, and quality checks. Each alert needs an owner, a dashboard or trace link, and a first action. A low-token output can still be wrong or unusable.

terms.definition: A value at or below which a stated fraction of observations falls.
The number of distinct label combinations in telemetry.
A measurable reliability or performance target over a stated window.

example: An invented support service targets 95% of responses under four seconds over a rolling day. A rise in retrieval latency triggers investigation of the index, while a simultaneous retry increase explains extra usage. Those thresholds are exercise assumptions, not industry guarantees.
mistakes: Reporting latency only for successful requests.
Adding every full prompt as a metric label.
Alerting without an owner or response procedure.
exercise: Create a monitoring plan with five metrics, their denominators, aggregation windows, and labels. Define one sustained-impact alert and a three-step investigation. State how you distinguish measured tokens from estimated cost.

questions.question: Why report a high latency percentile as well as the mean?
questions.answer: It reveals slower experiences that an average can obscure.
questions.distractor: It guarantees all users receive identical latency.

questions.question: Where should individual request IDs usually be inspected?
questions.answer: In traces or logs rather than as unbounded metric labels.
questions.distractor: As a new metric name for every request.

questions.question: Latency improves after failed requests are excluded. What should be reported?
questions.answer: The denominator change and failure rate, so the improvement is not misleading.

questions.question: What makes an alert actionable?
questions.answer: A defined impact, owner, evidence link, and initial response procedure.
questions.distractor: A notification with no context or responsible person.

questions.question: Does reduced token usage prove better application quality?
questions.answer: No. Quality and accepted-task outcomes need separate measurement.
questions.distractor: Yes, the shortest answer is always the best.
